correctness.rationale: Reconstruction of [1, Eq. (27)] gives the stated conservation and scalar Riccati equation. Uniform upper/lower risk comparisons force susceptible mass to zero off the initial layer. Exact integration by parts proves infected convergence. Moving-barrier Riccati comparison establishes the positive-time square-root diffusion rate. Dominated convergence yields the exact logarithmic susceptible coefficient. Continuous dependence proves the fast-time limiting ODE; its positive equilibrium attracts the fast layer. Numeric solver values at D=100, 10000, and 1000000 approach all three formulas, but analytic arguments, not those tests, establish the limit.

originality.rationale: The exact Gaussian SfIR equations and explicitly posed D-to-infinity problem occur in [1, Eq. (27), Section 5.1, lines corresponding to the open-problems paragraph]. The source gives time-to-infinity rather than diffusion-to-infinity results and conjectures infected density tends to zero at fixed positive time, contradicted by a uniform positive lower bound and the new explicit limit. [2] has different Gamma-type contact dynamics and a different kinetic scaling. Published-record searches and targeted mathematical searches found no theorem implying the explicit ODE asymptotic, fast-layer system, and sharp coefficient. This is a bounded evidence-based assessment, not a universal novelty guarantee.
residual_risks: Other unindexed publications or general fast-slow comparison theorems could subsume part of the result; searches cannot establish universal absence.
No limit for the full heterogeneous Fokker--Planck PDE is proved; its asymptotic question remains open.
One full-text earlier related article has different contact closure, so the present proof must not be read as covering every social-contact diffusion model.

value.rationale: The original study explicitly asks for the large-social-diffusion asymptotic of the Gaussian ODE and predicts a biologically different infection outcome. The theorem resolves all four bulk fields and the endogenous transmission variable for every fixed positive time, identifies and matches the nonlinear O(D^-1/2) initial layer, and derives a nontrivial exact large-deviation exponent for susceptible decay. These quantitative limits are needed to interpret strong behavioral diffusion and the order of epidemiological timescales. This is not a normalizing identity or a single-parameter numerical check.
